nameStory: The 'clammy' in clammy groundcherry comes from the sticky, somewhat gooey feel of the plant's stems and leaves when you touch them. The 'groundcherry' part refers to the papery lantern that surrounds the small fruit, which eventually drops to the ground and looks like a tiny cherry hiding in its protective case.
description: Clammy groundcherry is a low-growing herbaceous plant that belongs to the nightshade family, making it a cousin to tomatoes and peppers. This sprawling plant typically reaches 1-3 feet tall and has a somewhat weedy appearance with branching stems. It produces small yellow flowers that develop into cherry-sized fruits enclosed in inflated, papery husks that look like miniature Chinese lanterns. The entire plant has a distinctly sticky feel that gives it its common name.

idTips.label: Sticky Feel
idTips.description: The entire plant feels noticeably sticky or clammy to the touch, especially the stems and leaves. This tacky sensation will linger on your fingers after handling the plant.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pale yellow flowers about half an inch across with five petals and a dark purple-brown center. They hang downward from the leaf joints and have a bell-like shape.

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Small round fruits enclosed in papery, inflated husks that look like tiny paper lanterns. The husks are initially green but turn tan or brown as they mature.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Oval to heart-shaped leaves with wavy or slightly toothed edges, arranged alternately along the stem. They feel soft and somewhat fuzzy, adding to the plant's overall sticky texture.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Sprawling, somewhat weedy-looking plant that branches extensively and often appears to be lounging on the ground rather than standing upright.

habitat: Look for clammy groundcherry in disturbed areas like roadsides, vacant lots, and field edges throughout New England. It thrives in sandy or rocky soils and can tolerate dry conditions well. You'll often find it in waste places, old farm fields, and along railroad tracks where the soil has been disturbed.

seasonality.spring: Young plants emerge and begin growing, with the characteristic sticky stems becoming noticeable as temperatures warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak flowering occurs from June through August, with the small yellow flowers appearing throughout the growing season. Fruits begin developing in papery husks.
seasonality.fall: The papery lantern-like husks turn brown and may persist on the plant. Fruits ripen and the plant begins to die back with first frost.
seasonality.winter: Plant dies back completely, but dried husks may persist in the area as evidence of where plants grew the previous year.

funFact: Despite being called a 'cherry,' the fruit inside the papery husk is actually more closely related to a tiny tomato – and like many of its nightshade family relatives, the leaves and unripe fruits contain compounds that make them potentially toxic to eat.
confusionNotes: Clammy groundcherry can be confused with other groundcherry species, but the distinctly sticky feel of the entire plant is your best clue. Other groundcherries might be fuzzy or smooth, but none have that characteristic clammy, tacky sensation that persists on your fingers.
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name 'groundcherry' fool you into thinking these are related to actual cherries – they're nightshades through and through. While some groundcherry species produce edible fruits, it's best to admire clammy groundcherry rather than taste it, as proper identification between edible and potentially harmful species requires expertise.
compareHints: Among New England's groundcherries, clammy groundcherry stands out for its distinctly sticky texture – other species like hairy groundcherry are fuzzy but not sticky, while strawberry groundcherry tends to be more smooth. The clammy species also tends to be more sprawling and weedy-looking compared to its more upright relatives.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's groundcherries, strawberry groundcherry stands out for its distinctly fuzzy, gray-green appearance created by dense soft hairs.
